# Preface {.unnumbered}

Welcome! This book is a feature-by-feature guide to building Python web apps with Streamlit. It accompanies the Streamlit sessions in HSMA-7 (Health Service Modelling Associates Programme 7):

* [Module 2G: Creating a DES interface with Streamlit — Part 1](https://hsma-programme.github.io/hsma7_2g_streamlit_part1)
* [Module 2H: Creating a DES interface with Streamlit — Part 2](https://hsma-programme.github.io/hsma7_2h_streamlit_part2)

## How to use this book

In the module sessions, we build an interface for a discrete-event simulation (DES) model, introducing Streamlit features as we need them.

This book takes a different approach. It explores individual Streamlit features through focused explanations and examples, with less emphasis on DES. You can use it to revisit a topic from the sessions, try out a particular feature, or find an example to adapt for your own app.

If you are an HSMA student, we recommend following the module sessions to understand how the features fit together into a DES app, and using this book as a reference when you want to explore them individually.

You do not necessarily need to read the book from beginning to end: dip into the topics that are useful to you.

## stlite

Many examples in this book use the  [stlite](https://github.com/whitphx/stlite) framework and the [stlite extension for Quarto](https://github.com/whitphx/quarto-stlite), which allows example streamlit apps to run in your browser.

This does mean that the app examples within each page do take a while to load, and you may not want to read this book cover-to-cover if you are on, say, a mobile network - each example will load several megabytes of data to be able to render.

<br>

### Palmer Penguins

Several examples use the Palmer Penguins dataset, loaded through the [`palmerpenguins` Python package](https://github.com/mcnakhaee/palmerpenguins).

We thank Muhammad Chenariyan Nakhaee for the Python port, and Allison Horst, Alison Hill and Kristen Gorman for the [original R package](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/). The data were collected and made available by Dr Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) programme.

